items.followUp: Describe how Group-I metals react with water.

rubric.why: States the general product of the reaction with oxygen.
rubric.description: Group-I metals react with oxygen to form oxides.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the reaction forms an oxide (or oxygen-containing oxide).

rubric.why: A correct example equation supports the stated reaction.
rubric.description: Gives a correctly balanced example equation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct balanced equation for a Group-I metal reacting with oxygen.

modelAnswer: Group-I metals react with oxygen to form oxides.
For example: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O.

items.followUp: Explain why iodine is a solid while chlorine is a gas at room temperature.

rubric.why: Identifies bromine's state at room temperature.
rubric.description: States that bromine is a liquid at room temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying bromine as a liquid.

rubric.why: Links bromine's larger particles to stronger intermolecular attraction.
rubric.description: Explains that Br₂ molecules are larger than F₂ and Cl₂ molecules, so their intermolecular forces are stronger.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid explanation involving larger molecules, greater molecular mass, or more electrons.

modelAnswer: At room temperature, bromine is a liquid, whereas fluorine and chlorine are gases.
Br₂ molecules are larger and have more electrons than F₂ and Cl₂ molecules, so the intermolecular forces between Br₂ molecules are stronger.
More energy is therefore needed to separate Br₂ molecules, giving bromine a higher boiling point.

items.followUp: Write the formula of aluminium oxide using the valencies of aluminium and oxygen.

rubric.why: The first step is to identify the ions/elements and their combining capacities.
rubric.description: Writes the symbols and valencies (or charges) of the elements/ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying symbols and valencies, for example Al³⁺ and O²⁻.

rubric.why: Correct formula writing places the positive part before the negative part.
rubric.description: Writes the positive element or ion first and the negative element or ion second.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct order of the symbols.

rubric.why: Crossing the valencies gives the subscripts in the formula.
rubric.description: Crosses the valencies to become subscripts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly applying the criss-cross method.

rubric.why: Subscripts must express the simplest whole-number ratio.
rubric.description: Reduces the subscripts to the simplest whole-number ratio when necessary.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating or demonstrating reduction to the simplest ratio.

rubric.why: A correct example demonstrates the method and its final result.
rubric.description: Gives a correct formula as an example of the method.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct formula obtained using the method.

modelAnswer: Write the symbols of the elements or ions and note their valencies: Al³⁺ and O²⁻.
Write the positive symbol first and the negative symbol second: Al O.
Cross the valencies to become subscripts: Al₂O₃.
Reduce the subscripts to the simplest whole-number ratio if necessary; here they cannot be reduced.
Therefore, the formula of aluminium oxide is Al₂O₃.

items.followUp: Write four properties of cathode rays.

rubric.why: Canal rays are streams of positive ions.
rubric.description: States that canal rays consist of positively charged particles or ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the rays as positive ions.

rubric.why: Their straight-line travel is a characteristic property.
rubric.description: States that canal rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the straight-line property.

rubric.why: Their deflection in fields demonstrates their positive charge.
rubric.description: States that they are deflected by electric or magnetic fields, toward the negative plate in an electric field.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct statement about field deflection or the direction toward the negative plate.

rubric.why: Canal-ray particles are formed from the gas in the discharge tube, unlike electrons.
rubric.description: States that the nature or charge-to-mass ratio of canal-ray particles depends on the gas used.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the dependence on the gas used or an equivalent statement about variable particles.

modelAnswer: Canal rays are streams of positively charged particles (positive ions).
They travel in straight lines.
They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields; in an electric field they move toward the negative plate.
Their particles depend on the gas present in the discharge tube, so their mass and charge-to-mass ratio can vary.

items.followUp: Define ionic compounds and write four of their properties.

rubric.why: Covalent bonding is based on sharing electron pairs.
rubric.description: Defines covalent compounds as compounds whose atoms are bonded by sharing electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition that includes sharing of electrons between atoms.

rubric.why: Many simple covalent compounds have relatively weak forces between their molecules.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the low melting/boiling point property.

rubric.why: They generally do not have mobile charged particles to carry current.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds are poor conductors or do not conduct electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the electrical conductivity property.

rubric.why: Their solubility pattern is a characteristic property of many covalent compounds.
rubric.description: States that they are generally insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the solubility property.

rubric.why: Covalent substances occur in different physical states and are often gases, liquids, or soft solids.
rubric.description: States that many covalent compounds are gases, liquids, or soft solids at room temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the physical-state property.

modelAnswer: Covalent compounds are compounds in which atoms are held together by sharing one or more pairs of electrons.
They generally have low melting and boiling points.
They are generally poor conductors of electricity.
They are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
Many are gases or liquids, or are soft solids, at room temperature.

items.followUp: Explain how stronger intermolecular forces affect the boiling point of a liquid.

rubric.why: The nature and structure of a liquid determine the attractions between its particles.
rubric.description: States that boiling point depends on the nature or molecular structure of the liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating boiling point to the nature, structure, or polarity of the liquid.

rubric.why: Identifies intermolecular attraction as the relevant force to overcome during boiling.
rubric.description: Identifies intermolecular forces between liquid particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning intermolecular forces or attractions between molecules.

rubric.why: Boiling requires enough energy to overcome attractions between particles.
rubric.description: Explains that energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking boiling to overcoming the attractions.

rubric.why: The strength of attraction determines the relative boiling point.
rubric.description: States that stronger forces give a higher boiling point and weaker forces give a lower boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between force strength and boiling point.

modelAnswer: The boiling point depends on the nature of the liquid, because its molecular structure and polarity affect the attractions between its particles.
During boiling, energy must be supplied to overcome the intermolecular forces and separate the molecules.
A liquid with stronger intermolecular forces needs more energy to boil and therefore has a higher boiling point.
A liquid with weaker intermolecular forces needs less energy and has a lower boiling point.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a physical change and a chemical change.

rubric.why: A physical property can be observed without changing a substance's chemical identity.
rubric.description: Defines physical properties as observable or measurable without changing the substance's composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that composition or chemical identity remains unchanged.

rubric.why: A chemical property concerns the ability to undergo a change in chemical identity.
rubric.description: Defines chemical properties as describing a substance's ability to form new substances or change composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a chemical change alters composition or forms a new substance.

modelAnswer: A physical property can be observed or measured without changing the chemical composition or identity of a substance.
A chemical property describes how a substance can react to form new substances, changing its chemical composition.

items.followUp: What happens to an electron when it moves from a higher energy level to a lower one?

rubric.why: An electron moving to a lower energy level releases energy.
rubric.description: States that an electron emits energy when it moves from a higher energy level to a lower one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying emission during a downward transition.

rubric.why: An electron must gain energy to move to a higher energy level.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy when it moves from a lower energy level to a higher one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying absorption during an upward transition.

modelAnswer: An electron emits energy when it moves from a higher energy level to a lower energy level.
An electron absorbs energy when it moves from a lower energy level to a higher energy level.
